![Sabastian Sawe crosses the London Marathon finish line. Image from [BBC Sport](https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/articles/crm1m7e0zwzo).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Sabastian Sawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabastian_Sawe) ran 1:59:30 at the London Marathon, the first sub-two-hour finish in a record-eligible race. He took 65 seconds off [Kelvin Kiptum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Kiptum)'s 2023 world record; debutant [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha) came second at 1:59:41, and [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo) closed the podium in 2:00:28. Same day, [Tigst Assefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigst_Assefa) reset her own women's world record, [Marcel Hug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Hug) took his eighth London wheelchair title, and [Catherine Debrunner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Debrunner) won the women's wheelchair race on a sprint finish. [BBC Sport](https://www.bbc.com/sport/athletics/articles/crm1m7e0zwzo) has the men's-race focus; [The Guardian's live blog](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2026/apr/26/london-marathon-2026-live-updates) has the full four-race recap.

## My Notes

- Previously [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge) ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019, compared to Sawe's 1:59:30 in London.
- **Two** men broke two hours in the same race, and a third came within 28 seconds of the old record.
- London 2026 was a four-record day. Assefa's women's record, Hug's eighth wheelchair title, and Debrunner's sprint finish are each full stories on their own.
